title: Numbers, age & quantities
goal: Count, ask 'how many?' and 'how much?', give your age, and use ordinals like 'first' and 'second'.
intro:
First study the numbers chart: Tamil numbers 1–100 are quite regular once you know 1–10 and the tens. Remember that the spoken forms are shorter than the written ones — **ஒண்ணு** *oṇṇu* (1), **ரெண்டு** *reṇḍu* (2), **மூணு** *mūṇu* (3), **நாலு** *nālu* (4), **அஞ்சு** *anju* (5) — and these are what you will hear in every shop and bus.

In this unit you will use numbers with nouns, ask about quantity and age, and form ordinals with **-ஆவது** *-āvadu*.

vocab.note: spoken also நம்பர் nambar (phone number etc.)

phrases.en: How old are you? (lit. to you what age?)
I live on the third floor.

grammar.title: Numbers with nouns
grammar.body:
The number comes **before** the noun: மூணு புத்தகம் 'three books'. In speech the noun usually stays **singular** after a number (ரெண்டு காபி 'two coffees'); in writing the plural is common (மூன்று புத்தகங்கள்).

'One' before a noun is **ஒரு** *oru*, which also works as 'a/an': ஒரு காபி 'a coffee'. Standing alone, 'one' is ஒண்ணு. Similarly, many numbers have short combining forms in compounds (இரு-, மு-, நால்-, ஐ-), e.g. இருநூறு 'two hundred', ஐநூறு 'five hundred'.

For people, 'all three of us' etc. use **-உம்**: நாங்க மூணு பேரும் 'all three of us'. பேர் *pēr* is the counter for people: எத்தனை பேர்? 'how many people?'.

examples.en: There are five people in our house.

grammar.title: Asking quantity and age
grammar.body:
**எத்தனை** *ettanai* (spoken எத்தன) = 'how many' for things you count; **எவ்வளவு** *evvaḷavu* = 'how much' for amounts and prices.

Age uses the dative: **எனக்கு இருபது வயசு** 'to me twenty age' = 'I am twenty'. Ask politely with **உங்களுக்கு என்ன வயசு?** or **உங்களுக்கு எத்தன வயசு?**. (Asking adults their age is not rude in India, though you may want to avoid it with women older than you.)

examples.en: How many kilos do you want?
How much water do you need?

grammar.title: Ordinals with -ஆவது, and fractions
grammar.body:
Add **-ஆவது** *-āvadu* to a number to make an ordinal: மூணு → மூணாவது 'third', பத்து → பத்தாவது 'tenth'. The only exception is 'first', which is usually **முதல்** *mudal* (ஒண்ணாவது also exists for '1st standard' at school).

Fractions: **கால்** 'quarter', **அரை** 'half', **முக்கால்** 'three quarters'. Combine with -ஏ / -அரை: ரெண்டே கால் '2¼', ரெண்டரை '2½', ரெண்டே முக்கால் '2¾'. These are used constantly for time and weights.

dialogue.title: At the fruit stall
dialogue.setting: Sarah buys fruit from a street vendor (an older woman) in a Chennai market.

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.en: Come, madam! What would you like?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: How much for a dozen bananas?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: சரி, ஒரு டஜன் குடுங்க. மாம்பழம் கிலோ எவ்வளவு?
lines.roman: sari, oru ḍajan kuḍunga. māmbaḻam kilō evvaḷavu?
lines.en: OK, give me a dozen. How much are mangoes per kilo?

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.en: A hundred and twenty a kilo.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: Just half a kilo is enough.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: No, that's enough. How much altogether?

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.en: A hundred and twenty rupees in total.

culture: In speech, 'hundred' in compound numbers becomes நூத்தி *nūtti* (written நூற்றி): 120 = நூத்தி இருபது. Indians count large sums in **lakhs** (லட்சம், 100,000) and **crores** (கோடி, 10 million), written 1,00,000 and 1,00,00,000. When handing over money or objects, use your right hand; இந்தாங்க *indānga* 'here, take it' is the polite word.
